distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical source-context leaf for symptomatic urinary tract infection arising in the setting of an indwelling urethral catheter, intermittent catheterization, suprapubic catheter, nephrostomy drainage, recent catheter removal, or recurrent catheter manipulation. Organism, resistance pattern, obstructive uropathy, neurogenic bladder, urinary retention, bacteremia, urosepsis, renal abscess, and purple urine bag syndrome are context axes, treatment modifiers, event hazards, or future subtype/context structures rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: This leaf models symptomatic catheter-associated urinary infection and its catheter biofilm/source-control geometry. Pyelonephritis, acute prostatitis, urosepsis/bacteremia leaves, CLABSI, renal/perinephric abscess, asymptomatic bacteriuria/colonization, and noninfectious catheter obstruction or trauma remain near-neighbor manifolds or superposition candidates. Culture species, susceptibility, final source adjudication, and treatment response are confirmatory or treatment-context evidence unless a post-workup mode intentionally consumes them.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation-only ranking may consume catheter/device context, catheter dwell/manipulation, urinary retention or obstruction, suprapubic tenderness/pain, lower urinary tract symptoms, fever or blunted fever, delirium/altered mental status, vitals, CBC, CRP/PCT/lactate/renal labs, urinalysis, and presentation imaging. Urine/blood culture species, susceptibility, final source adjudication, and antibiotic response should be preserved but non-ranking in presentation tests.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Urinary catheter exposure, prolonged dwell time, urinary retention, neurogenic bladder, obstruction, frailty, diabetes, CKD, immunosuppression, poor mobility, constipation, and repeated catheter manipulation create the substrate for CAUTI.

Uropathogens adhere to catheter surfaces, drainage tubing, balloon, encrustations, sediment, or urinary device material, forming biofilm that shelters organisms from host clearance and antimicrobials.

Organisms ascend along the catheter lumen, external catheter surface, drainage system, periurethral tract, or catheterized stoma/nephrostomy tract, particularly after breaks in closed drainage or traumatic manipulation.

Replicating bacteria or Candida in catheterized urine and bladder mucosa drive bacteriuria, sediment, pyuria, catheter odor/cloudiness, culture positivity, and persistent infection when drainage or antibiotic coverage is inadequate.

Inflammation of bladder, urethral, catheter-tract, or occasionally upper-tract urothelium produces pyuria, leukocyte esterase, suprapubic tenderness, dysuria, urgency, hematuria, and catheter sediment/pus.

Bladder outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder, catheter blockage, encrustation, kinking, clot/sediment obstruction, hydronephrosis, or high residual urine sustains bacterial burden and increases AKI/source-control need.
Symptomatic CAUTI can drive fever, rigors, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin elevation, malaise, delirium, tachycardia, and sepsis physiology; frail or immunosuppressed hosts may have blunted symptoms.
Pathogens from catheterized lower or upper urinary tract can seed blood, causing hypotension, lactate elevation, AKI, respiratory failure, DIC-like coagulopathy, and mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Resistant or polymicrobial catheter uropathogen context
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Healthcare exposure and catheter biofilm increase probability of Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Proteus, ESBL/AmpC/CRE Enterobacterales, Candida, and polymicrobial infection, raising initial inactive therapy and recurrence risk.
Failure to remove, exchange, unblock, reposition, or otherwise control the infected catheter/device, obstructed drainage, or retained infected urine sustains infection despite antimicrobial exposure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: A urinary catheter or comparable urinary drainage device is the defining device context.
Longer dwell time raises colonization and biofilm risk.
Catheter dwell time, manipulation, drainage bag exposure, and host factors promote biofilm.
Biofilm and contaminated device surfaces seed organisms into bladder urine and mucosa.
Ascending organisms replicate in catheterized urine and device biofilm.
Stasis and retained urine support persistent bacterial burden.
Pathogen burden elicits pyuria and mucosal inflammation.
Symptomatic infection can produce systemic inflammatory response.
Heavy urinary burden or upper-tract/obstructed infection can seed blood.
Empirically missed or polymicrobial organisms prolong burden.
Retained infected catheter or uncorrected drainage failure continues seeding urine.
A retained infected catheter, obstruction, nephrostomy problem, or persistent retention creates source-control need.
Before exchange/removal/unblocking, source-control adequacy is low.
Compatible symptoms occurring with an active urinary catheter raise catheter-source probability.
Retention and high residual urine are central stasis mechanisms.
Obstructive uropathy or catheter malfunction sustains infection.
Kinking, blockage, sediment, encrustation, or traumatic removal can impair drainage.
Severe bladder outlet obstruction or drainage failure can produce hydronephrosis.
Inflamed infected urinary mucosa produces pyuria.
Urine WBC count rises with pyuria when reported quantitatively.
Routine urinalysis bacterial counts can be high in catheterized urinary infection.
Leukocyte esterase is a dipstick surrogate for urinary leukocytes.
Enterobacterales and some other nitrate reducers may produce nitrite; negative nitrite does not exclude CAUTI.
Catheter trauma, cystitis, stones, or obstruction can produce hematuria.
Bladder inflammation or retention causes suprapubic tenderness.
Bladder irritation may cause suprapubic pain, though symptoms can be absent in frail or catheterized hosts.
Dysuria can occur after catheter removal or with urethral/cystitis irritation but may be masked by catheterization.
Frequency or urgency can occur when bladder sensation and voiding are intact.
Urine culture positivity reflects pathogen burden but species identity remains confirmatory in presentation-only tests.
Healthcare and catheter exposure raise resistant uropathogen probability.
Long-term catheter biofilm increases Enterococcus and polymicrobial urine culture probability.
Resistance and polymicrobial context lower probability that empiric therapy is active.
Fever history is common in symptomatic CAUTI and urosepsis.
Pyrogenic inflammation raises measured temperature when host response is intact.
Bacterial urinary infection often causes leukocytosis, though response may be blunted.
CRP rises with systemic inflammation from symptomatic CAUTI.
PCT can rise with systemic bacterial infection or urosepsis.
Fever, pain, hypovolemia, and sepsis increase heart rate.
Older or neurologically vulnerable patients can present with delirium or altered mental status rather than classic urinary symptoms.
Urosepsis can produce positive blood cultures; species remains confirmatory in presentation-only ranking.
Distributive shock lowers blood pressure.
Urosepsis can lower MAP.
Shock and hypoperfusion raise lactate.
AKI may arise from obstruction, sepsis, dehydration, CKD background, or nephrotoxic therapy.
Obstruction and urosepsis raise AKI hazard.
Severe CAUTI can progress to septic shock.
Urinary pathogen burden can seed blood.
Mortality risk is driven by shock, AKI, bacteremia, source-control failure, resistant pathogens, and frailty.
Uncontrolled device/drainage source worsens urosepsis and recurrent infection risk.

In long-term catheterized patients, bacterial metabolism and plastic catheter-bag substrate can produce purple urine bag discoloration; this is a sign of catheterized UTI context, not a diagnosis label.

axes.shape_free_text: Current indwelling urethral Foley, suprapubic catheter, nephrostomy tube, intermittent catheterization need, or recently removed urinary catheter relevant to the episode.
Duration of urinary catheter exposure before the symptomatic episode.
Probability that the urinary catheter/device and catheterized bladder are the infectious source rather than another urinary or non-urinary source.
Catheter blockage, kinking, encrustation, sediment, leakage, traumatic self-removal, failed voiding trial, or drainage malfunction sustaining urinary stasis.
Urinary retention, inability to void, high residual urine, failed catheter removal, or catheter dependence.
Mechanical or functional urinary obstruction, bladder outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder stasis, or hydronephrosis-promoting drainage failure.
Degree of hydronephrosis or hydroureter attributable to obstructive uropathy or drainage failure during CAUTI context.
Bladder wall thickening, trabeculation, diverticula, cystitis appearance, turbid retained urine, or chronic obstructive bladder changes observed on imaging/cystoscopy.
Dysuria or burning urination, when the patient can perceive/void around the catheter or after catheter removal.
Frequency, urgency, bladder spasms, or irritative lower urinary tract symptoms in a catheterized or recently decatheterized patient.
Suprapubic pain or bladder discomfort.
Suprapubic tenderness on examination, which may reveal cystitis or retention even when the patient denies urinary symptoms.
Flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness suggesting upper-tract extension; overlaps with pyelonephritis and should not be used alone as a CAUTI label.
Qualitative pyuria, pus, urinary sediment with leukocytes, or positive urinary white-cell evidence.
Quantitative urine white blood cell count reported per microliter or equivalent converted unit.
Quantitative urinary bacteria count on routine urinalysis when reported.
Urine dipstick leukocyte esterase positivity.
Urine nitrite positivity; negative values do not exclude catheter-associated infection or Enterococcus/Pseudomonas/Candida contexts.
Gross or microscopic hematuria from catheter trauma, cystitis, obstruction, stones, or upper-tract involvement.
Dipstick or urinalysis proteinuria during catheterized infection; nonspecific and often kidney-background dependent.
Purple discoloration of a plastic urinary catheter bag in a catheterized patient, usually reflecting bacterial tryptophan metabolite chemistry in alkaline or colonized urine.
Probability that urine culture grows a clinically relevant organism in the acute episode; species and susceptibility are confirmatory/treatment-context evidence.
Urine culture quantitative growth, commonly high in catheter-associated infection but interpreted with symptoms and catheter context.
Probability that the catheter-associated uropathogen is resistant to ordinary empiric/narrow agents, including ESBL, AmpC, CRE, resistant Pseudomonas, VRE, MRSA, or resistant Candida contexts.
Probability that catheter biofilm infection is polymicrobial or includes Enterococcus, affecting coverage and interpretation of mixed urine culture.
Probability that current antimicrobial therapy is active and adequately dosed against the responsible catheter-associated urinary pathogen(s).
Need to adapt antimicrobial dosing or avoid nephrotoxicity because of CKD, AKI, obstruction, hemodialysis, or renal reserve.
Severe beta-lactam allergy or immediate hypersensitivity limiting standard gram-negative urinary coverage.
Measured body temperature; fever may be high, low-grade, or absent in frail catheterized hosts.
Reported fever, persistent fever, or fever during catheterized infection.
Heart rate; rises with fever, pain, dehydration, or urosepsis.
Systolic blood pressure; may fall with urosepsis or dehydration.
Mean arterial pressure; low values reflect shock unless supported.
Delirium, confusion, encephalopathy, reduced consciousness, or nonspecific altered mental status in a catheterized patient.
Peripheral white blood cell count; may be elevated, normal, or low depending host reserve.
C-reactive protein; elevated with systemic inflammation from symptomatic CAUTI.
Procalcitonin; often higher when CAUTI progresses to bacteremia or urosepsis.
Serum creatinine as renal function, obstructive uropathy, CKD, AKI, and antimicrobial dosing context.
Serum lactate; rises with septic shock and hypoperfusion.
Probability that blood cultures are positive during urosepsis; organism identity remains confirmatory/non-ranking in presentation tests.
Daily hazard of bacteremia arising from catheter-associated urinary infection.
Daily hazard of septic shock or circulatory collapse.
Daily hazard of AKI from obstruction, urosepsis, dehydration, CKD reserve, or nephrotoxic treatment.
Daily hazard of renal or perinephric abscess during complicated catheter-associated urinary infection; overlaps with pyelonephritis source-control pathways.

Lifespan outcome hazard for catheter-associated urinary tract infection; driven by septic shock, AKI, bacteremia, persistent obstruction/source-control failure, resistant pathogen context, frailty, and comorbidity.
Need for catheter removal, exchange, intermittent catheterization strategy, nephrostomy/stent/drainage intervention, or obstruction relief.
Adequacy of catheter removal/exchange/unblocking, bladder drainage, voiding restoration, upper-tract decompression, or other urinary source control.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The source probability is conditional on a relevant urinary device context.
Blocked or malfunctioning catheters require exchange, unblocking, or alternate drainage.
Adequate catheter/device control shortens ongoing culture positivity.
Adequate urinary drainage and device control lower severe outcome risk.
Qualitative pyuria and urine WBC count encode the same urinary inflammatory evidence at different granularity.
Leukocyte esterase and pyuria are linked urinalysis signals.
Hematuria may reflect catheter trauma, clot, stones, or mucosal injury that can worsen catheter function.
Fever and tachycardia often move together beyond shared mechanism means.
Inflammatory markers partially covary, though WBC may be blunted in frail or immunosuppressed hosts.
Septic shock is a central short-term mortality pathway.
AKI worsens prognosis and constrains antimicrobial dosing.
Bacteremic CAUTI has higher severe sepsis and mortality risk than localized cystitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removal/exchange vector only applies when a relevant urinary device is present.
A catheter cannot simply be removed if the patient cannot void or needs decompression.

failure_modes: retention or obstruction requiring continued drainage
upper-tract obstruction requiring nephrostomy or stent

side_effects.interpretation: Catheter exchange/removal can transiently increase traumatic hematuria.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control vector for suspected urinary catheter biofilm or drainage-source CAUTI.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Intermittent catheterization has less value when retention is absent.
Additional drainage strategy adds less after adequate source control.

failure_modes: unable to perform sterile intermittent catheterization

side_effects.interpretation: Intermittent catheterization can cause minor urethral trauma.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drainage/source-control strategy when permanent catheter removal is blocked by retention or neurogenic bladder.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibiotic vector requires activity against the causative organism(s).
ESBL/AmpC/CRE/Pseudomonas context can defeat ordinary empiric regimens.

side_effects.interpretation: Nephrotoxicity or renal-dose burden depends on chosen agent and renal reserve.

treatments.context_specific_role: Early antibacterial vector while culture and susceptibility context are clarified.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Broad resistant-pathogen coverage adds less when resistance context is weak.
Definitive susceptibility increases expected pathogen-burden reduction.

failure_modes: CRE or resistant non-fermenter not covered by selected agent

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity and dosing complexity depend on selected broad agent.

treatments.context_specific_role: Coverage lane for catheter-associated healthcare/resistant gram-negative or Pseudomonas/non-fermenter context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Enterococcus/gram-positive coverage adds less when ordinary gram-negative cystitis is most likely.
Vancomycin, aminopenicillins, linezolid, daptomycin, or other choices require context-specific dosing/toxicity review.

side_effects.interpretation: Some gram-positive regimens carry renal or monitoring burdens.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add-on/definitive lane when Enterococcus or gram-positive catheter-associated urinary pathogen context is plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Upper-tract decompression helps when obstruction/hydronephrosis is clinically relevant.
Benefit is largest when antibiotics cannot control an obstructed infected system.

side_effects.interpretation: Upper-tract drainage procedures can cause transient hematuria.

treatments.context_specific_role: Emergency source-control lane for obstructive CAUTI, hydronephrosis, pyonephrosis concern, or failed lower-tract drainage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support matters when shock is present or imminent.
Support does not sterilize urine or catheter biofilm.

failure_modes: persistent shock if antimicrobial/source control delayed
fluid overload in CKD or heart failure

side_effects.interpretation: Fluid/vasopressor strategy can interact with renal and cardiac reserve.

treatments.context_specific_role: State support while antimicrobial and urinary source-control vector fields take effect.

present.clinical_rationale: A urinary catheter is the defining source-context risk.
Long dwell time and drainage-system breaks promote biofilm and resistant/polymicrobial colonization.
Stasis and high residual urine amplify infection persistence and AKI risk.
Trauma, obstruction, or recurrent catheter manipulation can inoculate organisms and impair drainage.
Frail catheterized patients often have nonspecific or blunted presentations and worse outcomes.
Renal background changes creatinine interpretation, dosing, and complication hazard.
Host immune/metabolic vulnerability and antibiotic selection increase resistant infection and severe outcomes.
Constipation and immobility promote retention, long catheter exposure, and PUBS-type catheterized UTI signs.
Inactive or delayed coverage sustains pathogen burden and increases dissemination risk.
Retained infected device or persistent obstruction prolongs infection and worsens severe outcome risk.

supportive_care: Confirm that symptoms or systemic signs are present; asymptomatic bacteriuria or colonization in a catheterized patient should not be treated as this symptomatic disease manifold without compatible clinical evidence.
Obtain urinalysis and urine culture from a freshly replaced catheter or appropriate sampling port when feasible; do not delay antibiotics in sepsis.

Preserve culture species, susceptibility, colony counts, catheter-tip cultures, and final source adjudication as confirmatory or treatment-context evidence unless the workflow intentionally uses post-workup evidence.
Assess the urinary device: indication, dwell time, drainage-system integrity, obstruction, sediment/encrustation, leakage, trauma, repeated self-removal, and whether removal or exchange is feasible.
Remove or exchange the catheter when it is no longer necessary; if drainage is still required, use the least biofilm-sustaining safe strategy and reassess the need daily.
Evaluate urinary retention, neurogenic bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, hydronephrosis, nephrostomy/stent need, and failed voiding trials as source-control context rather than diagnostic labels.
Monitor fever, mental status, blood pressure, lactate, WBC, CRP/PCT, creatinine, urine output, and electrolytes in severe or frail presentations.
Use renal-dose adjustment and toxicity monitoring for antimicrobials in CKD, AKI, obstruction, or older adults.
Escalate to sepsis resuscitation, ICU monitoring, blood cultures, and urologic source control when shock, AKI, obstruction, or persistent fever occurs.
quality_notes: No treatment-rank labels are encoded; treatment ranking should emerge from active coverage, source control, obstruction, renal reserve, and sepsis-state axes.
Catheter type, organism, resistance, upper-tract obstruction, urosepsis, bacteremia, and purple urine bag syndrome are modeled as context/axis structures rather than disease-name qualifiers.
